faqs.q: What should I include on a pressure washing estimate?
faqs.a: At minimum: your business name, the client and property address, a dated surface-by-surface list (driveway, house exterior, deck, fence, sidewalk), a validity date, deposit terms, and a note that it is not a final invoice.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate the deposit automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantities and rates, and the subtotal, 25% deposit and balance due update automatically.

faqs.q: Is this legal or tax advice?
faqs.a: No. Templates are for informational purposes only. Requirements vary by state — verify with your contractor board and a CPA or attorney before use.

deepDive.heading: How pressure washing jobs are actually priced
deepDive.sub: Surface type drives both the price and the pressure. The same square footage is worth four times as much on a roof as on a driveway, and using the driveway setting on a roof is how contractors buy their customers new shingles.

blocks.h3: The pricing basis: surface, not square footage
paras: Concrete flatwork is the baseline: driveways and sidewalks typically run $0.15 to $0.35 per square foot, or $100 to $300 for a standard driveway. House washing is priced per square foot of exterior wall at $0.20 to $0.50, or as a flat $150 to $400 for a typical single-family home. Roofs soft-washed run $0.30 to $0.60 per square foot because the work is slower and the liability is higher.

Fences, decks and patios break the square-foot model entirely. A fence is priced per linear foot because both sides may need cleaning, and a wooden deck per square foot but at a much lower pressure with a different chemical. Quoting all of it at one per-square-foot rate is how a job ends up unprofitable on the fence and overpriced on the driveway.
list: Driveway / flatwork: $0.15–0.35 per sq ft, $100–300 typical
House wash: $0.20–0.50 per sq ft of wall, $150–400 typical
Fence: $1.50–3.00 per linear foot, both sides extra

blocks.h3: Pressure limits are a legal exposure, not a preference
paras: Concrete tolerates 3,000 to 4,000 PSI. Wood siding and decks should stay under about 1,200 PSI or the grain lifts. Stucco and painted surfaces usually want under 1,500 PSI with a wide fan tip, and asphalt shingles should never see more than about 100 PSI — which is why roofs are soft-washed with a chemical and low pressure rather than blasted.

Put the method on the estimate, not just the price. 'Roof soft wash at low pressure with sodium hypochlorite' sets an expectation and protects you when a customer asks why their neighbour's roof was power washed at high pressure. It also justifies a price that looks higher than a competitor who is about to damage the shingles.

A pressure washer consumes 2 to 4 gallons per minute, so a 30-minute house wash can use over 100 gallons. Most residential jobs run off the customer's spigot, but jobs without water access need a tank and a pump, which is a real cost that belongs on the estimate as its own line.

Some jurisdictions require wash water recovery, particularly where runoff reaches storm drains. If reclaim is required, that equipment and time change the price significantly. Chemicals — sodium hypochlorite, surfactants, rust remover — are typically 5 to 10 percent of the job price and are the line most often forgotten when a contractor wins a bid that was too cheap.
steps: Confirm water access and flow rate before quoting.
Check whether the jurisdiction requires reclaim for this runoff path.
Price the chemical mix as a separate material line.
State the method and pressure range on the estimate.
Note that pre-existing damage (chipped paint, loose flashing) is documented before work starts.

blocks.h3: Recurring work is where the margin is
paras: A one-off house wash is a commodity. A twice-yearly maintenance contract with the same customer, invoiced the same way each visit, is a business. Price the maintenance visit 10 to 20 percent below the one-off rate to make the commitment worthwhile, and the customer stops shopping the price each season.

Invoice lines should match the surfaces: house wash, driveway, walkways, deck, gutter brightening, chemical treatment. Keeping them separate makes it obvious what was done on each visit, and makes it easy to add or drop a surface without renegotiating the whole price.
